gloss_terse: much, many, great; enough; abounding in; chief — quantitative and qualitative abundance, sufficiency, or rank
gloss_readable: One of the most versatile adjectives in biblical Hebrew, rav spans a wide arc from simple counting ('many people,' 'much water') to qualitative greatness ('great wickedness,' Gen 6:5), to the exclamatory 'Enough!' that God speaks to Israel at Horeb (Deut 1:6). In construct it yields the rich idiom 'abounding in steadfast love' (Exod 34:6), a phrase that became central to Israel's creedal confession. Arabic kathir, Spanish mucho/grande, and Korean manheun/keun all split across the same quantitative-qualitative divide, confirming that the word genuinely straddles two conceptual territories rather than being a single vague term.

senses.1: The dominant sense across 305 occurrences, functioning as a straightforward quantitative adjective: 'many days' (Gen 21:34), 'much livestock' (Gen 26:14). Arabic kathir and Spanish muchos/mucho align precisely. The word modifies both count nouns (many people) and mass nouns (much wealth), paralleling the Hindi bahut / Swahili -engi split.
senses.2: A qualitative sense appearing about 65 times, where rav marks greatness in intensity, importance, or moral weight rather than mere quantity. 'The wickedness of man was great' (Gen 6:5) and 'their sin is very great' (Gen 18:20) illustrate the shift. Korean keun and Arabic azim map here, while German gross captures the qualitative force that viel does not.
senses.3: In construct with a following noun, rav means 'abounding in' or 'rich in' (19x). The creedal formula rav-hesed 'abounding in steadfast love' (Exod 34:6; Num 14:18; Neh 9:17) is the prime example. Spanish abundante-de and Arabic kathiru + genitive both require a distinct grammatical frame, confirming this as a real sense boundary.
senses.4: An exclamatory or adverbial use meaning 'enough! sufficient!' (14x), as in Jacob's cry 'Enough! Joseph my son is still alive' (Gen 45:28) and God's command rav lakhem 'You have stayed long enough' (Deut 1:6). Arabic kafa, Swahili -tosha, and Spanish basta all translate with a different lexeme than 'many,' showing genuine semantic specialization.
senses.5: A comparative sense (10x) meaning 'greater, more numerous,' as in the oracle 'the elder shall serve the younger' (Gen 25:23) and 'those who are with us are more' (2 Kgs 6:16). Spanish mayor/mas and German der Altere reflect the comparative function that cross-linguistically requires distinct morphology.
senses.6: An adverbial extension (8x) conveying degree or temporal extent: 'greatly' (Ps 62:2; 123:3) or 'long' (Ps 120:6; 1 Kgs 19:7). Korean kheuge/orae and Swahili sana/muda mrefu use separate adverbs, distinguishing this from the adjectival senses.
senses.7: A nominalized use (5x) meaning 'abundance, multitude, greatness,' typically in construct or after prepositions: 'by the greatness of your power' (Job 23:6), 'the abundance of his steadfast love' (Isa 63:7). Arabic kathra and Swahili wingi occupy a distinct nominal slot.
senses.8: Verbal forms (4x) where rav functions as a predicate meaning 'became many, increased, multiplied' (Exod 23:29; 1 Sam 14:19; 2 Sam 15:12). Korean manahjida and Swahili kuongezeka show how languages treat this as a process verb rather than an adjective of state.
senses.9: A rare substantival title (2x) meaning 'chief, captain, master' — rav used as a rank designation in Prov 26:10 and Jer 52:24. Arabic rais, Korean janggwan, and Swahili mkuu all supply a distinct noun for officialdom, indicating a frozen lexical specialization.
senses.10: A single occurrence in Isa 19:20 where rav appears in the phrase 'a great one who will defend them,' possibly a title or epithet. English 'defender,' Spanish grande, and French nombreux diverge enough to suggest textual or semantic uncertainty.

gloss_terse: stretch out, spread, extend; incline, bend, turn aside; pitch a tent; pervert justice
gloss_readable: A root of physical gesture and moral direction, natah pictures the extension of God's arm in judgment (Exod 7:5), the spreading of heavens like a tent curtain (Isa 40:22), and the bending of a heart toward obedience or away from it. The same root that describes pitching a tent at Bethel (Gen 12:8) also describes perverting justice at the gate (Deut 16:19). Arabic nataa 'stretch,' maala 'incline,' and nasaba 'pitch' each claim a different slice of the semantic space, confirming that Hebrew natah genuinely fuses extension, inclination, and deviation under one lexeme.

senses.1: The core Qal transitive sense (45x): physically stretching out the hand or arm, overwhelmingly in divine action — 'I will stretch out My hand' (Exod 7:5). Moses stretching his staff over Egypt (Exod 8:5-6, 8:16) is the paradigm. Arabic madda and Spanish extender map cleanly, while Korean ppeotda uses a dedicated verb for bodily extension.
senses.2: Hifil causative (37x): inclining the ear or heart toward God, instruction, or a petition. 'Incline your ear' (2 Kgs 19:16; Ps 17:6) and 'incline their hearts to Him' (1 Kgs 8:58) are the representative frames. Arabic amala 'cause to lean' and Korean giulida both require a causative morpheme, mirroring the Hebrew binyan shift.
senses.3: Qal passive participle (30x): the iconic 'outstretched arm' of the Exodus formula — 'with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm' (Deut 4:34; 5:15; 7:19). Arabic mamduda and Spanish extendida render this as a stative adjective, confirming its participial, adjectival character distinct from the active verb.
senses.4: Intransitive Qal (24x): turning aside from a path or moral standard without external cause — 'Judah went down and turned aside to an Adullamite' (Gen 38:1), 'they turned aside after dishonest gain' (1 Sam 8:3). Arabic maala and Spanish apartarse capture the self-directed deviation.
senses.5: Hifil causative turning aside (21x): causing someone or something to deviate — Balaam's donkey turned aside (Num 22:23), Joab turned Abner aside (2 Sam 3:27). Arabic hawwala and Spanish apartar distinguish the causative agent from intransitive deviation in sense 4.
senses.6: Intransitive Qal inclining or bowing (16x): shadows declining (Judg 19:8), a person bowing under a burden (Gen 49:15), divine favor inclining toward someone (Gen 39:21). Arabic maala / inhadara and Korean giulda cover this physical-directional meaning. Distinct from sense 4 because no departure or deviation is implied.
senses.7: Hifil forms specialized for perverting justice (14x): 'you shall not pervert justice' (Exod 23:2, 6; Deut 16:19; 24:17; 27:19). Arabic harrafa 'distort' and Spanish torcer 'twist' show that cross-linguistically, legal distortion recruits a distinct lexeme. This moral narrowing of the causative 'turn aside' sense is a genuine biblical idiom.
senses.8: Qal active participle (12x) describing the one who stretches out or spreads — preeminently God stretching out the heavens (Job 9:8; Isa 40:22; 44:24; Ps 104:2). Arabic nashara/basata 'spread out' and Spanish el que extiende confirm a cosmic-creative frame distinct from the hand-extension of sense 1.
senses.9: A concrete Qal application (10x): pitching a tent or tabernacle — 'Abram pitched his tent' (Gen 12:8; 26:25; 33:19). Arabic nasaba 'erect' and French dresser supply specialized verbs, indicating this is a distinct collocational sense tied to the tent-culture setting.
senses.10: Miscellaneous Qal finite forms (7x) meaning to spread out or extend physically — wings, branches, heavens, shadows lengthening (Num 24:6; Job 15:29; Isa 45:12; Jer 10:12). These overlap with senses 1 and 8 but involve territorial or cosmic spreading without the hand/arm frame or participial morphology.

gloss_terse: uncover, strip bare; reveal, disclose; go into exile, deport; depart, vanish
gloss_readable: A root that moves between exposure and expulsion, galah links the physical act of uncovering nakedness (Lev 18) with the theological act of divine self-revelation (Gen 35:7; 1 Sam 3:21) and the catastrophic experience of exile (2 Kgs 17:23). The connection is not accidental: to be 'uncovered' is to be laid bare before a hostile world, which is precisely what exile does to a nation. Arabic kashafa 'uncover/reveal' and jalaa 'emigrate' preserve the same dual semantic axis, while Korean beotgida (strip) and yubae (exile) split into entirely separate words.

senses.1: Piel factitive (40x): physically uncovering, stripping bare, or removing a covering — overwhelmingly in the Levitical nakedness laws (Lev 18:6-19). Arabic kashafa and Hindi ughaarna both denote physical exposure. The Piel intensifies the action: not merely opening but completely stripping away a covering.
senses.2: Hifil causative (38x): to exile or deport a population — the engine of prophetic judgment. 'The king of Assyria exiled Israel' (2 Kgs 17:6; 15:29; 16:9). Arabic ajlaa/sabaa and Swahili kupeleka uhamishoni use distinct verbs, confirming that forced deportation is semantically separate from voluntary departure (sense 4).
senses.3: Nifal reflexive-passive (33x): to be revealed, appear, or manifest oneself, including God's theophanies — 'God revealed Himself to him at Bethel' (Gen 35:7), 'the glory of the LORD shall be revealed' (Isa 40:5). Arabic inkashafa 'become uncovered' and Korean deureonada 'come to light' capture the passive self-disclosure dimension.
senses.4: Intransitive Qal (22x): to go into exile voluntarily or under compulsion, including the substantive participle goleh 'an exile.' 'My people go into exile for lack of knowledge' (Isa 5:13). Arabic jalaa 'emigrate' preserves the intransitive Qal sense that the Hifil (sense 2) makes causative.
senses.5: Piel factitive applied to information (16x): to reveal secrets, disclose plans, make divine truths known — 'He reveals deep things out of darkness' (Job 12:22), 'the heavens shall reveal his iniquity' (Job 20:27). Arabic kashafa in abstract contexts and Hindi prakat karna both extend 'uncovering' to intellectual disclosure.
senses.6: Transitive Qal (15x): to reveal or disclose, overlapping with Piel sense 5 but in the simpler stem — 'the LORD revealed to Samuel' (1 Sam 9:15), 'I thought to disclose it to you' (Ruth 4:4). The Qal-Piel distinction may reflect intensity: Qal for ordinary disclosure, Piel for dramatic revelation.
senses.7: Hofal passive (7x): to be exiled or deported by an external agent — 'Judah was exiled' (1 Chr 9:1), 'Mordecai who had been exiled' (Esth 2:6). The passive of the Hifil (sense 2), cross-linguistically rendered by passive forms: Arabic juliya, Korean japyeogatda.
senses.8: Qal passive participle (7x): the state of being open, uncovered, or exposed — Balaam with 'eyes uncovered' (Num 24:4, 16), 'open rebuke' (Prov 27:5), letters 'published openly' (Esth 3:14). Arabic makshuf and Korean yeollin/deureonan mark the stative-adjectival function.
senses.9: Intransitive Qal (6x): to depart or vanish without the exile frame — 'the glory has departed from Israel' (1 Sam 4:21-22), 'the produce of the field departs' (Prov 27:25). Arabic irtahala 'depart' and Korean tteonada distinguish simple leaving from the politically charged exile of senses 2, 4, and 7.
senses.10: Hitpael reflexive (2x): to uncover oneself, with connotations of shameful self-exposure — Noah 'uncovered himself' in drunkenness (Gen 9:21), and the fool 'lays bare' his heart (Prov 18:2). Arabic reflexive inkashafa and Korean beotgyeojyeotda confirm the self-directed, often pejorative coloring.

gloss_terse: open a door, gate, or container; loose bonds, set free; draw a sword; open mouth or eyes
gloss_readable: The primary Hebrew verb for opening, patah covers the full range from opening a sack in Egypt (Gen 42:27) to opening the windows of heaven in the Flood (Gen 7:11) to loosing the bonds of captives in Babylon (Isa 52:2). Its Piel intensification yields 'loose, untie,' extending naturally to 'set free' — a semantic path that Arabic fataha, Spanish abrir/soltar, and Korean yeolda/pulda each handle with different lexemes. The root's versatility makes it a key term in both narrative action and prophetic promise.

senses.1: The basic Qal transitive sense (67x): opening a physical object — a door (Gen 8:6), a sack (Gen 42:27), a gate (Josh 10:22), storehouses (Gen 41:56). Arabic fataha, Korean yeolda, Swahili -fungua, and Spanish abrir converge precisely, making this the cross-linguistically most stable sense.
senses.2: Nifal passive (14x): to be opened — 'the windows of heaven were opened' (Gen 7:11), 'the doors of the temple were opened' (Neh 7:3). Arabic infataha and Korean yeollida supply regular passive morphology. Job 32:19 ('wineskins about to burst') shows the Nifal shading toward spontaneous opening.
senses.3: Piel intensive (14x): to loose, untie, or unbind — loosening camels' harness (Gen 24:32), unbuckling armor (1 Kgs 20:11), loosing the bonds of kings (Job 12:18). Arabic halla/fakka 'untie' and Korean pulda 'loosen' are distinct from 'open,' confirming the Piel specialization beyond simple opening.
senses.4: Qal passive participle (13x): the state of standing open — 'your eyes may be open' toward this house (1 Kgs 8:29, 52), a city left open (Josh 8:17), an open grave (Jer 5:16). Arabic maftuh and Spanish abierto function as stative adjectives, distinct from the dynamic Nifal 'be opened' (sense 2).
senses.5: Qal with body-part objects (13x): opening the mouth, lips, or eyes — 'you shall open wide your hand' (Deut 15:8, 11), the speechless opening his mouth (Prov 31:8), Ehud's servants waiting until embarrassed (Judg 3:25). Korean ibul yeolda and Arabic fataha famahu show that body-part collocations form a recognizable sub-pattern.
senses.6: Piel applied to persons (6x): to set free or release from captivity — 'He brings out prisoners into prosperity' (Ps 68:6), 'He sent and released him' (Ps 105:20). Arabic atlaqaa 'release' and Korean noajuda 'let go' employ a different verb than 'open,' confirming the liberation sense as a genuine Piel extension beyond physical untying (sense 3).
senses.7: Qal/Nifal intransitive (4x): to open wide or break forth — the earth 'opened its mouth' (Ps 106:17), ears 'shall be unstopped' (Isa 35:5), the heavens 'break forth' (Isa 45:8). Korean teojirira 'burst' and Swahili -funguka mark this as spontaneous or dramatic opening without a human agent.
senses.8: Hitpael reflexive (2x): to loose oneself from bonds — 'Loose yourself from the chains on your neck' (Isa 52:2, twice in Qere/Ketiv). Arabic inhalli and Korean pulla confirm the reflexive morphology. A rare but theologically potent form in the context of Zion's liberation.
senses.9: A specialized Qal sense (2x): drawing a sword from its sheath — 'the wicked have drawn the sword' (Ps 37:14), 'a drawn sword' (Ezek 21:28). Arabic salla 'unsheathe' and Spanish desenvainaron use a dedicated military term. The metaphor of opening a covering extends naturally to unsheathing a blade.
senses.10: A single occurrence (Isa 5:27) where the meaning is debated: 'none whose sandal-strap is loosened.' English 'is loosened,' Spanish se desatara, and German oeffnen diverge, suggesting either a variant of the Piel 'loose' sense or a textual difficulty. The context describes an invading army whose equipment never fails.
